taxonomyNote: NatureServe notes that some authors place Sistrurus within Crotalus because Crotalus is paraphyletic without it; the genus name Sistrurus is still in standard use.
fieldMarks: Small rattlesnake, usually 38-64 cm; grey, tan, brown or reddish with alternating dark mid-dorsal and lateral blotches and an orange-brown dorsal stripe in some.
Dark stripe from the eye to the corner of the mouth, heat-sensing pit between eye and nostril, keeled scales, single anal plate.
Tiny rattle with a faint buzz like a grasshopper, audible only about a yard away; juveniles have a bright yellow tail tip that darkens with age.
behavior: Solitary, reclusive and sedentary, sheltering under logs, brush, stumps or in small-mammal burrows; will flee but may strike if cornered.
Ambush predator that eats lizards, snakes, frogs, insects, centipedes, nestling birds and small mammals; juveniles lure prey with the tail tip.
In Florida seen most often July-November; in the north activity peaks June-September.
habitat: Mainly moist or wet lowlands: wet prairies and savannas, pine flatwoods, swamps, floodplains, sandhills and pond or canal edges; in Missouri, south-facing rocky partly wooded hillsides.
range: Southeastern and south-central United States: Alabama, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Kentucky, Louisiana, Missouri, Mississippi, North Carolina, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Tennessee and Texas; not in Canada.

lookalikes.name: Timber rattlesnake
lookalikes.howToTell: Adults are 3-5 ft long with a large rattle, versus a tiny rattle on the pygmy rattlesnake (Missouri Department of Conservation).
